**KPRM** (870 AM) is a radio station in Park Rapids, Minnesota. It has a hybrid adult contemporary/conservative talk radioformat. Locally, it broadcasts the popular "Coffee Talk" morning show, and is currently simulcasted on KDKK.

National news comes from the Fox News, the News/Talk/Sports and More format is locally owned and operated. Sports from Westwood One and Premiere Networks' Clay Travis and Buck Sexton Show and _The Sean Hannity Show_.
On November 30, 2016, KPRM was granted an FCCconstruction permit to increase the night power to 2,500 watts.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KPRM#cite_note-3) KPRM can also be heard on four cross-service FM translators: 100.5 MHz Park Rapids, 96.3 MHz Walker, 103.1 MHz Bemidji and 94.7 Staples/Wadena.
In October 2021, KPRM changed its music segments from classic country to adult contemporary. KPRM continues to carry News/Talk, Sports and More. The more being adult contemporary music.
KPRM transmits with 50,000 watts of power during the day, 1,000 watts at night, and is owned and operated by De La Hunt Broadcasting, through licensee De La Hunt Media, Inc. The studios and offices are on the east side of Park Rapids, near the intersection of Highways 34 and 4. Because WWL in New Orleans, Louisiana is the dominant Class A station on 870 AM, KPRM must reduce power during nighttime hours, preventing interference with the skywave signal of WWL.
In 2006, previous owners Ed and Carol De La Hunt were inducted into the Pavek Museum of Broadcasting Hall of Fame.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KPRM#cite_note-4) Effective September 24, 2021, ownership of KPRM and its sister stations was transferred to Ed and Tamara De La Hunt.
In addition to the Park Rapids properties (KPRM, KDKK 97.5, and KXKK 92.5), they also own KKWB 102.5 in Bemidji, Minnesota, KAKK 1570 and KQKK 101.9 in Walker, Minnesota.

**KPRM** (870 AM) is a radio station in Park Rapids, Minnesota. It has a hybrid adult contemporary/conservative talk radioformat. Locally, it broadcasts the popular "Coffee Talk" morning show, and is currently simulcasted on KDKK.

National news comes from the Fox News, the News/Talk/Sports and More format is locally owned and operated. Sports from Westwood One and Premiere Networks' Clay Travis and Buck Sexton Show and _The Sean Hannity Show_.
On November 30, 2016, KPRM was granted an FCCconstruction permit to increase the night power to 2,500 watts.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KPRM#cite_note-3) KPRM can also be heard on four cross-service FM translators: 100.5 MHz Park Rapids, 96.3 MHz Walker, 103.1 MHz Bemidji and 94.7 Staples/Wadena.
In October 2021, KPRM changed its music segments from classic country to adult contemporary. KPRM continues to carry News/Talk, Sports and More. The more being adult contemporary music.
KPRM transmits with 50,000 watts of power during the day, 1,000 watts at night, and is owned and operated by De La Hunt Broadcasting, through licensee De La Hunt Media, Inc. The studios and offices are on the east side of Park Rapids, near the intersection of Highways 34 and 4. Because WWL in New Orleans, Louisiana is the dominant Class A station on 870 AM, KPRM must reduce power during nighttime hours, preventing interference with the skywave signal of WWL.
In 2006, previous owners Ed and Carol De La Hunt were inducted into the Pavek Museum of Broadcasting Hall of Fame.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KPRM#cite_note-4) Effective September 24, 2021, ownership of KPRM and its sister stations was transferred to Ed and Tamara De La Hunt.
In addition to the Park Rapids properties (KPRM, KDKK 97.5, and KXKK 92.5), they also own KKWB 102.5 in Bemidji, Minnesota, KAKK 1570 and KQKK 101.9 in Walker, Minnesota.

**Park Rapids** is a city in and the county seat of Hubbard County, Minnesota, United States.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-GR6-5) It is near Itasca State Park, the source of the Mississippi River,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-6) as well as the beginning of the Heartland State Trail.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-Heartland_State_Trail:_Minnesota-7) The city was founded in 1890 near the Fish Hook River rapids[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-Warren_Upham_2008_pp._244-8) and is along U.S. Highway 71 and Minnesota State Highway 34.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-9) The population was 4,142 at the 2020 census.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-2020_Census_(City)-2)
Steam hauler moving logs along snow on skids

The land that is now Park Rapids was originally inhabited by Native American tribes, including the Ojibwe (Chippewa) people, who still have a significant presence in the region.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-10) Park Rapids became a city in 1882, and was named by Frank C. Rice after the park groves and prairies beside the Fish Hook River rapids. These rapids have since been dammed.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-Warren_Upham_2008_pp._244-8) Located at the convergence of prairie and pine forest, Park Rapids emerged as a supply depot for farmers and the lumber industry. It was a crucial hub for trappers, the local Ojibwe community, and timber cruisers to exchange goods, report, and replenished supplies. Later, Park Rapids grew into a logging center, with numerous trails leading north for tote teams transporting goods. Its main street was made unusually wide to accommodate the long, horse-drawn teams essential to the town's operations.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-11)
Park Rapids and the surrounding Hubbard County area have three major transportation services. South of the city center at 212 W. 2nd Street is Park Rapids Municipal Airport (officially Konshok Field), a general aviation airport.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-12) According to the FAA, the airfield is publicly owned by the City of Park Rapids. Also serving the Park Rapids and Hubbard County area for ground transportation is the Hubbard County Heartland Express[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-13) bus service and a local taxi service. The closest commercial airport is Bemidji Regional Airport, which is served only by Delta Connection flights to Minneapolis–Saint Paul International Airport, about 200 miles from Park Rapids.

U.S. Highway 71 and Minnesota State Highway 34 are two of the main routes through Park Rapids. Highway 34 was expanded in 2008 into a five-lane route through the city.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-14) Downtown Main Avenue has street "center parking". Highway 71 and Main Street were reconstructed in 2009.
According to the United States Census Bureau, the city has an area of 6.81 square miles (17.64 km 2), of which 6.59 square miles (17.07 km 2) is land and 0.22 square miles (0.57 km 2) is water.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-Gazetteer_files-15) The Fish Hook River flows through the city, which is surrounded by three lakes: Fish Hook, Long, and Potato.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-16)
Park Rapids has a humid continental climate (Köppen_Dwb_), with warm summers and long, cold snowy winters.

**Park Rapids** is a city in and the county seat of Hubbard County, Minnesota, United States.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-GR6-5) It is near Itasca State Park, the source of the Mississippi River,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-6) as well as the beginning of the Heartland State Trail.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-Heartland_State_Trail:_Minnesota-7) The city was founded in 1890 near the Fish Hook River rapids[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-Warren_Upham_2008_pp._244-8) and is along U.S. Highway 71 and Minnesota State Highway 34.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-9) The population was 4,142 at the 2020 census.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-2020_Census_(City)-2)
Steam hauler moving logs along snow on skids
texts.2:
The land that is now Park Rapids was originally inhabited by Native American tribes, including the Ojibwe (Chippewa) people, who still have a significant presence in the region.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-10) Park Rapids became a city in 1882, and was named by Frank C. Rice after the park groves and prairies beside the Fish Hook River rapids. These rapids have since been dammed.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-Warren_Upham_2008_pp._244-8) Located at the convergence of prairie and pine forest, Park Rapids emerged as a supply depot for farmers and the lumber industry. It was a crucial hub for trappers, the local Ojibwe community, and timber cruisers to exchange goods, report, and replenished supplies. Later, Park Rapids grew into a logging center, with numerous trails leading north for tote teams transporting goods. Its main street was made unusually wide to accommodate the long, horse-drawn teams essential to the town's operations.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-11)
Park Rapids and the surrounding Hubbard County area have three major transportation services. South of the city center at 212 W. 2nd Street is Park Rapids Municipal Airport (officially Konshok Field), a general aviation airport.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-12) According to the FAA, the airfield is publicly owned by the City of Park Rapids. Also serving the Park Rapids and Hubbard County area for ground transportation is the Hubbard County Heartland Express[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-13) bus service and a local taxi service. The closest commercial airport is Bemidji Regional Airport, which is served only by Delta Connection flights to Minneapolis–Saint Paul International Airport, about 200 miles from Park Rapids.
texts.3:
U.S. Highway 71 and Minnesota State Highway 34 are two of the main routes through Park Rapids. Highway 34 was expanded in 2008 into a five-lane route through the city.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-14) Downtown Main Avenue has street "center parking". Highway 71 and Main Street were reconstructed in 2009.
According to the United States Census Bureau, the city has an area of 6.81 square miles (17.64 km 2), of which 6.59 square miles (17.07 km 2) is land and 0.22 square miles (0.57 km 2) is water.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-Gazetteer_files-15) The Fish Hook River flows through the city, which is surrounded by three lakes: Fish Hook, Long, and Potato.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-16)
Park Rapids has a humid continental climate (Köppen_Dwb_), with warm summers and long, cold snowy winters.

**Park Rapids** is a city in and the county seat of Hubbard County, Minnesota, United States.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-GR6-5) It is near Itasca State Park, the source of the Mississippi River,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-6) as well as the beginning of the Heartland State Trail.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-Heartland_State_Trail:_Minnesota-7) The city was founded in 1890 near the Fish Hook River rapids[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-Warren_Upham_2008_pp._244-8) and is along U.S. Highway 71 and Minnesota State Highway 34.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-9) The population was 4,142 at the 2020 census.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-2020_Census_(City)-2)
Steam hauler moving logs along snow on skids

The land that is now Park Rapids was originally inhabited by Native American tribes, including the Ojibwe (Chippewa) people, who still have a significant presence in the region.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-10) Park Rapids became a city in 1882, and was named by Frank C. Rice after the park groves and prairies beside the Fish Hook River rapids. These rapids have since been dammed.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-Warren_Upham_2008_pp._244-8) Located at the convergence of prairie and pine forest, Park Rapids emerged as a supply depot for farmers and the lumber industry. It was a crucial hub for trappers, the local Ojibwe community, and timber cruisers to exchange goods, report, and replenished supplies. Later, Park Rapids grew into a logging center, with numerous trails leading north for tote teams transporting goods. Its main street was made unusually wide to accommodate the long, horse-drawn teams essential to the town's operations.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-11)
Park Rapids and the surrounding Hubbard County area have three major transportation services. South of the city center at 212 W. 2nd Street is Park Rapids Municipal Airport (officially Konshok Field), a general aviation airport.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-12) According to the FAA, the airfield is publicly owned by the City of Park Rapids. Also serving the Park Rapids and Hubbard County area for ground transportation is the Hubbard County Heartland Express[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-13) bus service and a local taxi service. The closest commercial airport is Bemidji Regional Airport, which is served only by Delta Connection flights to Minneapolis–Saint Paul International Airport, about 200 miles from Park Rapids.

U.S. Highway 71 and Minnesota State Highway 34 are two of the main routes through Park Rapids. Highway 34 was expanded in 2008 into a five-lane route through the city.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-14) Downtown Main Avenue has street "center parking". Highway 71 and Main Street were reconstructed in 2009.
According to the United States Census Bureau, the city has an area of 6.81 square miles (17.64 km 2), of which 6.59 square miles (17.07 km 2) is land and 0.22 square miles (0.57 km 2) is water.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-Gazetteer_files-15) The Fish Hook River flows through the city, which is surrounded by three lakes: Fish Hook, Long, and Potato.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Rapids,_Minnesota#cite_note-16)
Park Rapids has a humid continental climate (Köppen_Dwb_), with warm summers and long, cold snowy winters.

**Hubbard County** is a county in the northwestern part of the U.S. state of Minnesota. As of the 2020 census, the population was 21,344,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubbard_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-2020_Census_(City)-1) and it was estimated to be 22,369 in 2025.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubbard_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-QF-2) Its county seat is Park Rapids.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubbard_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-3)
Part of the Leech Lake Indian Reservation is in Hubbard County.
The county was created on February 26, 1883,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubbard_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-4) with territory partitioned from Cass County. It was named for Lucius Frederick Hubbard, a prominent Territory editor, Civil War participant, and businessman who was governor of Minnesota from 1882 to 1887.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubbard_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubbard_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-6) The county's boundaries have remained unchanged since its creation.
The new county's courthouse was destroyed by fire around 1890, but the public records were salvaged.
The county's terrain is hilly, largely wooded, and dotted with lakes and ponds.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubbard_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-HCM-7) It generally slopes to the east, with the northern part sloping to the north and the southern part sloping to the south. Its highest point is near the lower middle of its western border, at 1,549 ft (472 m) ASL.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubbard_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-8)

According to the United States Census Bureau, the county has an area of 999.500 square miles (2,588.69 km 2), of which 926.021 square miles (2,398.38 km 2) is land and 73.479 square miles (190.31 km 2) (7.35%) is water.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubbard_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-9) It is Minnesota's 24th-largest county by area.
The Forest Service maintains a tower at the Thorpe Lookout, with an elevation of 1,844 feet.
